author: historian-agent:mig-1
title: Lapita expansion into Remote Oceania
summary: The Lapita culture, known for dentate-stamped pottery and associated with Austronesian speakers, appears in the Bismarck Archipelago about 3,300 years ago. Within a few centuries its voyagers settled previously uninhabited islands in Melanesia and West Polynesia, reaching Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji and Tonga.

uncertainty.note: Years are 1950 minus cal BP, taking midpoints. Bismarcks 3360-3240 cal BP (Denham et al. 2012, cited by Petchey et al. 2015, who argue charcoal-based dates overestimate antiquity). New Caledonia: Vatcha occupation "shortly after 3000 cal BP"; the authors note slightly earlier occupation is likely. Teouma: most likely start 2920-2870 cal BP (68.2%); maximum range 3000-2560. Tonga: first Lapita landfall 2846-2839 cal BP. Fiji (Naigani 3019-2863; Bourewa 2838-2787) overlaps Teouma and Tonga and is mentioned but not a waypoint because it would break the date order.

as_recorded.value: Earliest possible Lapita appearance in the Bismarck region 3360-3240 cal BP (Denham et al., cited)
Vatcha (Isle of Pines, New Caledonia) occupied shortly after 3000 cal BP (Sheppard et al., cited)
Teouma Lapita most likely start 2920-2870 cal BP; colonization of Tonga 2850-2830 cal BP and Fiji 3020-2860 cal BP
Lapita appeared in the Bismarck Archipelago by ~3,350-3,150 BP; individuals from Vanuatu 3,000-2,800 BP and Tonga 2,700-2,300 BP linked to Lapita
The Lapita expansion occurred between 1600 and 1000 BC

where.modern_name: Bismarck Archipelago, Papua New Guinea (first waypoint)
where.historical_name: Near Oceania at the edge of Remote Oceania; no recorded place names

waypoints.date: 3360-3240 cal BP (Bismarck Archipelago; Denham et al. via Petchey et al. 2015)
waypoints.label: Bismarck Archipelago, Papua New Guinea: earliest Lapita appearance. Point is the archipelago centroid; the Mussau Islands and other sites are not named in the opened source.

waypoints.date: shortly after 3000 cal BP (Vatcha, Isle of Pines; Sheppard et al. via Petchey et al. 2015). Slightly earlier occupation likely
waypoints.label: Isle of Pines, New Caledonia: Vatcha site occupation. Point is the island centre; slightly earlier occupation is suspected but not securely dated.

waypoints.date: most likely start 2920-2870 cal BP (68.2% prob.; Teouma, Petchey et al. 2015)
waypoints.label: Teouma, Efate, Vanuatu: Lapita settlement and cemetery.

waypoints.date: first Lapita landfall 2846-2839 cal BP (Tonga; Burley et al. via Petchey et al. 2015)
waypoints.label: Tonga: earliest Lapita landfall, Bayesian-modelled. Point is Tongatapu; the specific site is not named in the opened source.

importance.justification: The first settlement of Remote Oceania, which opened the way to the later colonisation of Polynesia.

related.because: Lapita voyagers descend from the Austronesian expansion into the Pacific.
West Polynesia was the staging area for the later settlement of East Polynesia.

reviewer_note: Least sure: Fiji and Samoa are not waypoints (Fiji dates overlap Teouma/Tonga; no opened source dates Samoa); the Bismarck point is a centroid and its date is an upper bound that Petchey et al. consider too old; Vatcha is "shortly after 3000" approximate; Tonga site not named. The Oxford Handbook and ANU Press sources are reused from the Austronesian record.

beats.caption: Lapita pottery first appears in the Bismarck Archipelago, north of New Guinea, from about 3,300 years ago.
Voyagers settle New Caledonia and Efate in Vanuatu, where the Teouma site was founded about 2,900 years ago.
Lapita people land in Tonga about 2,840 years ago, extending settlement far into Remote Oceania.
